title: Anchannock
summary: Anchannock is Tooker's recorded Indigenous name for Robins Island in Peconic Bay. The name is interpreted as land well wooded or full of timber.
address_label: Robins Island, Peconic Bay, Southold, NY
why_this_matters: Anchannock preserves an Indigenous name for Robins Island in Peconic Bay, with an interpretation tied to land that was well wooded or full of timber. That meaning points to the practical ways Native place names can describe ecology, resources, and how people understood island landscapes. Read beside the modern English name, Anchannock keeps older layers of Peconic Bay language and memory present.
introduction_content: Anchannock is the recorded name for Robins Island in Peconic Bay, within Southold town. The existing polygon represents the modern island, which is the supported geographic association for the placename.
translation_content:
The name is interpreted Anchannock as land well wooded or full of timber, drawing on related Algonquian language comparisons. The interpretation is Tooker's historical linguistic reading rather than a settled modern translation.

Why Place Names Matter

“Replacing colonial place names with Indigenous place names does not erase history, but rather corrects it.”

— Christina Gray and Andrew Ambers, The Rematriation of Indigenous Place Names (2026), Introduction
whereintheworld_content: Anchannock preserves an Indigenous name for an island whose wooded character mattered in a region where wood became scarce early in colonial settlement. Together, the name connects Robins Island to Native place memory, deed history, and environmental context.
